module

public import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Erdős Problem 288

*Reference:* [erdosproblems.com/288](https://www.erdosproblems.com/288)
-/

@[expose] public section

namespace Erdos288

/--
Is it true that there are only finitely many pairs of intervals $I_1$, $I_2$ such that
$$
\sum_{n_1 \in I_1} \frac{1}{n_1} + \sum_{n_2 \in I_2} \frac{1}{n_2} \in \mathbb{N}?
$$
-/
@[category research open, AMS 11]
theorem erdos_288 : answer(sorry) ↔ Set.Finite { I : Fin 2 → ℕ+ × ℕ+ |
    ∀ j, (I j).1 ≤ (I j).2 ∧
      ∃ n : ℕ+, (∑ j : Fin 2, ∑ nⱼ ∈ Set.Icc (I j).1 (I j).2, (nⱼ⁻¹ : ℚ)) = n } := by
  sorry

/--
This is still open even if $|I_2| = 1$.
-/
@[category research open, AMS 11]
theorem erdos_288.variants.i2_card_eq_1 : answer(sorry) ↔ Set.Finite { (I, n₂) : (ℕ+ × ℕ+) × ℕ+ |
    I.1 ≤ I.2 ∧ ∃ n : ℕ+, ∑ n₁ ∈ Set.Icc I.1 I.2, (n₁⁻¹ : ℚ) + (n₂⁻¹ : ℚ) = n } := by
  sorry

/--
It is perhaps true with two intervals replaced by any $k$ intervals.
-/
@[category research open, AMS 11]
theorem erdos_288.variants.k_intervals : answer(sorry) ↔ ∀ k, Set.Finite { I : Fin k → ℕ+ × ℕ+ |
    ∀ j, (I j).1 ≤ (I j).2 ∧
      ∃ n : ℕ+, (∑ j : Fin k, ∑ nⱼ ∈ Set.Icc (I j).1 (I j).2, (nⱼ⁻¹ : ℚ)) = n } := by
  sorry

/--
Is it true for any $k > 2$ that only finitely many $k$ intervals satisfy this condition?
-/
@[category research open, AMS 11]
theorem erdos_288.variants.exists_k_gt_2 : answer(sorry) ↔
    ∃ k > 2, Set.Finite { I : Fin k → ℕ+ × ℕ+ |
      ∀ j, (I j).1 ≤ (I j).2 ∧
        ∃ n : ℕ+, (∑ j : Fin k, ∑ nⱼ ∈ Set.Icc (I j).1 (I j).2, (nⱼ⁻¹ : ℚ)) = n } := by
  sorry

end Erdos288

findings.description: The source does not pose this variant. Its docstring, "Is it true for any $k > 2$ that only finitely many $k$ intervals satisfy this condition?", is not website text, and the Lean reads it existentially: `∃ k > 2, Set.Finite {…}`. The source's only remark about k intervals is universal, and `erdos_288.variants.k_intervals` already formalizes it correctly as `∀ k`. Appending the interval {1} maps the (k−1)-interval solution set injectively into the k-interval one (proved in scratch: `mono`, `exists_iff_three`). So this right-hand side is exactly finiteness for k = 3. It is strictly between the main problem and the ∀k variant: a meaningful, non-trivial open question, but the formalizer's own intermediate question rather than the source's. The docstring is also ambiguous: under the equally natural reading "for every k > 2", the Lean `∃` contradicts it (and that reading would just duplicate `k_intervals`). The ErdosProblems README asks that variants come from the website's additional text and that docstrings quote it. Mathematically the statement is fine; the issue is attribution and wording, so a maintainer should decide whether to keep it.
findings.source_evidence: erdosproblems.com/288 (snapshots 2025-09-10 and 2026-07-09), the only k-remark: "It is perhaps true with two intervals replaced by any $k$ intervals." Erdős–Graham 1980, p. 34 makes it explicitly universal: "Perhaps for each k, Σ_{i=1}^k Σ_{a_i,b_i} can be an integer only finitely often." Neither source asks whether it holds for some k > 2.
findings.suggested_fix: Remove the variant, since `k_intervals` already states the source's claim. Or keep it but say explicitly that it is not in the source, e.g. docstring "Is there some $k > 2$ such that only finitely many $k$-tuples of intervals have integer reciprocal sum? (Not stated in the source; it is implied by `k_intervals` and implies `erdos_288`; equivalent to the case $k = 3$.)". Optionally state it directly for `Fin 3`.

reformulations.difference: The Lean ranges over ordered pairs `Fin 2 → ℕ+ × ℕ+` of nonempty integer intervals [a,b], a ≤ b. It allows I₁ = I₂ and overlapping intervals. The source just says "pairs of intervals" (the book: "Σ_{a,b} + Σ_{c,d} is an integer only finitely often") and never says "disjoint", so the Lean follows it literally. A reader might still assume disjointness was intended.
reformulations.equivalence_argument:
Ordered versus unordered changes the count by at most a factor 2, and each nonempty interval of positive integers has exactly one encoding. If disjointness were intended, the Lean set differs from the disjoint one only by overlapping pairs, and only finitely many of those have an integer sum. For overlapping I₁, I₂, the sum is Σ_{n∈U} c_n/n, where U = I₁∪I₂ = [a,b] is an interval of length L and c_n ∈ {1,2}.
- If L ≥ 2 and a > L: Sylvester–Schur gives a prime p > L ≥ 2 dividing exactly one m ∈ U. Since p ∤ c_m, v_p(sum) = −v_p(m) < 0.
- If a ≤ L: Bertrand gives a prime p ∈ (b/2, b]. It lies in U and is its only multiple of p, and p ≥ 3 unless b ≤ 2, so again v_p(sum) < 0.
- If L = 1: the sum is 2/a, an integer only for a ≤ 2.
So the only overlapping solutions are ({1},{1}), ({2},{2}), ([1,2],[1,2]), ([1,2],{2}) and ({2},[1,2]). An exhaustive search of all pairs with endpoints ≤ 2000 found exactly these, plus the disjoint solutions {[1,3],{6}}, {[2,3],{6}} and {[3,6],{20}}. The disjoint and non-disjoint readings are therefore equally finite or infinite.

reformulations.difference: The singleton I₂ = {n₂} may lie inside I₁. Also, ordered pairs (I, n₂) are counted rather than unordered pairs of intervals.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: When n₂ ∈ I₁, the sum is Σ_{n∈I₁} c_n/n with c_n ∈ {1,2}, so the argument used for `erdos_288` (Sylvester–Schur plus Bertrand) applies. It leaves only ({1},1), ({2},2) and ([1,2],2), a finite set. So the Lean set is finite exactly when the set of pairs with |I₂| = 1 (disjoint or not) is finite. The sum parses as `(∑ n₁ ∈ Icc, 1/n₁) + 1/n₂`, since the body is `term:67`; the example ([3,6],20) was checked to lie in the set.

reformulations.difference: The condition is `∀ j, (I j).1 ≤ (I j).2 ∧ ∃ n : ℕ+, (∑ j, …) = n`. The integrality conjunct sits inside `∀ j`, and the inner `∑ j` shadows the outer `j`. For k = 0 the Lean set is therefore all of `Fin 0 → ℕ+ × ℕ+`, not the empty set that `(∀ j, …) ∧ ∃ n, 0 = n` would give.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: For k ≥ 1, `Fin k` is nonempty and the conjunct does not depend on the outer j, so the set equals {I | (∀ j, (I j).1 ≤ (I j).2) ∧ ∃ n, sum = n}. For k = 0 the ambient type is a singleton, so both sets are finite. Finiteness is therefore unchanged for every k (proved in scratch: `S_eq_S'`, `finite_iff`). The same pattern in `erdos_288` and `exists_k_gt_2` is harmless, since there k ≥ 2.

sources_consulted: https://mathweb.ucsd.edu/~ronspubs/80_11_number_theory.pdf — P. Erdős, R. L. Graham, Old and New Problems and Results in Combinatorial Number Theory (1980), p. 34 (scanned; OCR'd locally)

review.notes:
No status issues. erdosproblems.com still lists #288 as OPEN (snapshot of 2026-07-09: "There are no solutions, partial or complete, claimed in the comments"). The teorth/erdosproblems database also says open. So `research open` is correct for all four declarations.

The main theorem, `i2_card_eq_1` and `k_intervals` are faithful:
- The answer polarity is correct.
- ℕ+ endpoints avoid the 1/0 junk value, and `a ≤ b` rules out empty intervals.
- `∃ n : ℕ+` is equivalent to membership in ℕ, because the sum is positive.

Lean checks in /workspace/review:
- The website/book example 1/3+1/4+1/5+1/6+1/20 = 1 lies in both the main set and the `i2_card_eq_1` set (`decide +kernel`).
- The chain k_intervals ⟹ exists_k_gt_2 ⟹ erdos_288 holds.
- The right-hand side of `exists_k_gt_2` is equivalent to finiteness for k = 3 (append the interval {1}).

Caveat for k ≥ 3: the Lean k-interval sets allow overlapping or repeated intervals. This matches the literal source (Σ_{i=1}^k Σ_{a_i,b_i}), but unlike the k = 2 case I have not shown it equivalent to a pairwise-disjoint reading. A search of triples with endpoints ≤ 90 found no degenerate infinite family.

Minor, not a mathematics issue: the module docstring cites only erdosproblems.com and not the original source [ErGr80], which the ErdosProblems README asks to be listed.

I did not read the erdosproblems forum thread (7 comments), to avoid discussions of this repository's file. The page summary already records that no solutions are claimed there.
